title: Leonel A. Regalado Cardoso
text:
I am a Ph.D. student in the Department of Agricultural and Applied Economics at Texas Tech University and a Research Assistant at the Free Market Institute. I also serve as a Graduate Instructor in the Area of Energy Commerce & Business Economics at the Rawls College of Business.
I earned my B.A. in Economics from Universidad Francisco Marroquín and completed a Postgraduate Certificate in Money, Banking, and Central Banking at The University of Buckingham. My research focuses on migration, entrepreneurship, and political economy, with an emphasis on how institutions, policy environments, and economic incentives influence individual behavior and long-run development outcomes. More broadly, my work seeks to understand how institutional changes shape economic opportunity and entrepreneurial activity across countries and regions.

Migration Working Paper


Did the Syrian Refugee Crisis destroy European economic freedom?


with Benjamin Powell



A growing body of theoretical work argues that large-scale immigration from institutionally weaker countries could erode the institutional quality of destination countries. The logic is straightforward: if immigrants carry the cultural attitudes, political preferences, and institutional norms of their home countries, and if those norms are hostile to economic freedom, then sufficiently large inflows could shift destination-country policies in a statist direction. This “new economic case for immigration restrictions”, advanced by Borjas (2015), Collier (2013), and others, has become one of the most prominent arguments against open borders. Yet the empirical evidence for institutional erosion remains thin.


The Syrian refugee crisis provides what should be the hardest possible test for institutional resilience. The institutional gap is enormous: Syria scored 4.53 on the Economic Freedom of the World index while the major European host countries scored approximately 8.0, a gap of more than 3.5 points on a 10-point scale. Unlike voluntary economic migrants, refugees are less self-selected on attitudes toward destination-country institutions; they are fleeing conflict, not choosing destinations based on economic or institutional preferences. And the scale was unprecedented in modern European history: Germany absorbed over one million Syrians, Sweden took in a share equivalent to 2.2% of its population, and Austria received inflows that fundamentally altered its demographic composition.


We apply the synthetic control method to construct counterfactual institutional trajectories for the three treated countries, specifically Germany, Austria, and Sweden, using a donor pool of 21 European countries where the Syrian-born population remained below 0.1% of the total. Countries between 0.1% and 0.5% are excluded to ensure clean separation. For each treated country, we construct a weighted combination of donor countries that best matches the pre-treatment trajectory of the EFW index along with covariates including the Gini coefficient, GDP per capita, civil liberties, and human capital. The most notable donors in the synthetic counterfactuals are the United Kingdom (carrying 47% of Austria’s weight, 57% of Germany’s, and 39% of Sweden’s), the Czech Republic, France, Ireland, and Poland. We then stack the three country-level analyses by aligning treatment years and averaging effects.






Stacked synthetic control: treated countries versus their synthetic counterfactual. Hover over the lines to see exact EFW values at each period.





Post-treatment effects with p-values. Hover over each bar to see the exact treatment effect and statistical significance.



The results are unambiguous: the Syrian refugee surge did not meaningfully impact destination countries’ economic freedom. In the stacked analysis, all post-treatment point estimates are negative but small; the largest gap is just 0.18 points in period 6, and most are statistically insignificant. Only period 6 reaches conventional significance (p = 0.05), and the joint p-value through year 6 is 0.106. At the country level, Sweden is the most striking case: despite having the highest refugee-to-population ratio and the fastest naturalization pathway (58% of Syrians naturalized by 2023), it shows no statistically significant effect in any post-treatment year.


The findings are robust across three alternative specifications: using all pre-treatment lags without covariates (following Ferman et al., 2020), dropping the United Kingdom from the donor pool to address potential Brexit contamination, and adding immigrant stock as an additional covariate. In every case, the substantive conclusion is the same: the estimated effects are economically trivial and statistically indistinguishable from zero.


This paper contributes to a growing literature that consistently fails to find evidence of institutional erosion from immigration. The Syrian case is particularly informative because the theoretical conditions for detecting erosion are maximally favorable: large institutional gap, low self-selection, rapid inflows. If institutional erosion were going to happen anywhere, it should have happened here. That it did not suggests that the mechanisms through which immigrants theoretically degrade institutions, including direct political participation, welfare state expansion, erosion of social trust, or shifting native voter preferences, either do not operate or offset each other in practice. The “new economic case for immigration restrictions” remains a theoretical possibility without empirical support.






Entrepreneurship Working Paper


Do corruption reforms spur entrepreneurship?


 



Corruption is widely seen as one of the most important obstacles to economic development, and anti-corruption reform is a central pillar of the international development agenda. Pavlik et al. (2023) provided compelling causal evidence that sustained improvements in corruption control lead to economic growth. But growth through what channel? One natural candidate is entrepreneurship: if corruption raises the cost of doing business through bribes, unpredictable regulation, and legal uncertainty, then reducing corruption should lower barriers to entry and encourage new business creation. This paper tests that hypothesis directly.


The empirical challenge is substantial. Most existing studies of corruption and entrepreneurship rely on cross-sectional or standard panel regressions that cannot address the fundamental identification problem: countries that reform corruption differ systematically from those that do not. Moreover, anti-corruption reforms are adopted at different times across countries, creating a staggered treatment structure that renders traditional two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences (DiD) estimates biased. The now well-documented problem of “forbidden comparisons”, using already-treated units as controls for later-treated units, can produce misleading estimates when treatment effects are heterogeneous across cohorts.


This paper addresses both problems by applying the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) DiD estimator, which properly handles staggered treatment adoption by computing group-time-specific average treatment effects using only not-yet-treated or never-treated units as controls. Treatment is defined as a sustained 5-year improvement of more than 0.20 in the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators Control of Corruption index, with the additional constraint that any single-year decrease during that window does not exceed 0.07. This definition filters out transient fluctuations and captures meaningful, durable institutional change.





Event study for formal firm registrations (World Bank data): pre-treatment trends support parallel trends, but post-treatment effects are consistently negative and statistically insignificant.





Event study for total early-stage entrepreneurial activity (GEM data): no discernible change in either direction after anti-corruption reform.




The analysis draws on two complementary datasets. The World Bank Group Entrepreneurship Survey provides data on formal firm registrations per 1,000 working-age people, a measure that captures only businesses entering the formal sector. The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) provides broader measures of entrepreneurial activity, including total early-stage entrepreneurship (TEA), opportunity-driven TEA, necessity-driven TEA, and the opportunity-to-necessity ratio, which capture both formal and informal ventures. The World Bank sample identifies 20 treated countries with treatment years between 2011 and 2016; the GEM sample identifies 10 treated countries between 2007 and 2016.


The results are strikingly consistent: anti-corruption reforms have no statistically significant effect on any measure of entrepreneurship. Formal firm registrations show a slight negative point estimate (ATT = −0.70, s.e. = 0.54), and the event study plots show a persistent but insignificant downward drift after treatment. The pre-treatment periods show confidence intervals consistently including zero, supporting the parallel trends assumption. Total TEA from GEM is essentially flat (ATT = −0.51, s.e. = 1.42). Opportunity-driven TEA is negative but insignificant (−1.95, s.e. = 1.17). Necessity-driven TEA shows the largest negative point estimate (−2.68, s.e. = 1.80) but remains insignificant. The opportunity-to-necessity ratio is slightly positive (+0.36) but also insignificant.


The divergence between the World Bank results (slight decline in formal registrations) and the GEM results (no change in total activity) is itself informative. It suggests that anti-corruption reforms may temporarily reshape the form of entrepreneurship rather than its level, shifting activity between formal and informal sectors as entrepreneurs adapt to stricter enforcement, new licensing requirements, and regulatory restructuring, without changing the overall rate of business creation. The formal decline likely reflects short-term administrative disruption rather than a genuine contraction in entrepreneurial dynamism. The implication for the growth literature is clear: the economic gains documented by Pavlik et al. must flow through channels other than entrepreneurial entry, such as investment, human capital accumulation, structural transformation, or productivity improvements within existing firms.






Migration Published


Emigration and origin country economic institutions


with Benjamin Powell · Public Choice, 2025



One of the most important questions in development economics is whether emigration helps or hurts the countries people leave behind. Standard analyses focus on remittances, brain drain, and labor market effects, but institutions are arguably the most fundamental determinant of long-run prosperity. If emigration systematically changes economic institutions in origin countries, the welfare implications could dwarf the direct effects that dominate the literature.


This paper provides the first systematic test of the nonlinear relationship between emigration and economic institutions. Drawing on public choice theory and Hirschman’s exit-voice framework, we identify four distinct channels. The absence channel predicts that emigration worsens institutions: people who are most dissatisfied with the status quo leave, shifting the median voter toward those who tolerate poor governance. The prospect channel works in the opposite direction: governments facing outflows of productive citizens have an incentive to reform in order to retain their tax base. The diaspora channel operates through social remittances: emigrants living under better institutions transmit liberal norms, ideas, and political preferences back home. Finally, the return channel captures the direct impact of returnees who bring human capital, resources, and changed worldviews acquired abroad.


These channels need not operate with equal force at all levels of emigration. At moderate levels, the diaspora and return channels should dominate; enough people abroad to generate institutional spillovers, but not so many that the absence channel overwhelms them. At very high levels of emigration, however, the sheer depletion of human capital and civic participation could reverse the gains. This logic predicts an inverted-U relationship.


We test this using panel data on emigration from 132 countries to 20 OECD destinations between 1980 and 2010, drawn from the Institute for Employment Research’s Brain Drain dataset. The dependent variable is the 10-year change in the Economic Freedom of the World (EFW) index, which captures the quality of economic institutions across five dimensions: size of government, legal system and property rights, sound money, freedom to trade internationally, and regulation. Our specifications include two-way fixed effects, quadratic terms, skill-specific disaggregation, and instrumental variables for flow regressions.





Predicted total effect of emigrant stock on EFW change, showing the inverted-U relationship peaking near 20% of the population abroad.





Skill-specific effects: medium- and high-skill emigrant stocks drive institutional improvements, with high-skill effects never turning negative within the observed range.




The results confirm the inverted-U hypothesis. Larger emigrant stocks are positively and significantly associated with subsequent improvements in economic freedom, but the squared term is negative and significant. The relationship peaks at about 20% of the population living abroad, where the estimated association is a 0.90-point improvement on the 10-point EFW scale. Only at extreme levels (above 47%) does the total effect turn negative, and only Guyana exceeds that threshold. Crucially, this positive association is larger for countries with weaker initial institutions, exactly as the diaspora channel would predict: the greater the gap between origin and destination country institutions, the larger the potential for institutional convergence.


Disaggregating by skill reveals that medium- and high-skill emigrant stocks drive the result. High-skill emigration, in particular, never turns negative within the observed data range, suggesting that the human capital embodied in high-skill emigrants generates persistent institutional spillovers through the diaspora and return channels. Contemporaneous emigration flows, by contrast, show no significant relationship with institutional change, providing no evidence that the prospect channel operates in the aggregate. Instrumental variable estimates using a shift-share instrument confirm that the negative OLS association between high-skill flows and institutional quality is driven by reverse causality.


The policy implications are substantial. Allowing greater emigration from low-economic-freedom countries to high-economic-freedom countries could promote development not only through the standard channels of remittances and human capital accumulation, but through a previously underappreciated mechanism: institutional improvement in origin countries. This adds a new dimension to the already enormous estimated global gains from freer migration.






Entrepreneurship Published


Property rights and entrepreneurship


Economic Affairs, 45(3), 509-521, 2025



Property rights are widely regarded as a cornerstone of entrepreneurial activity. Secure ownership, enforceable contracts, and the rule of law reduce uncertainty, lower transaction costs, and allow entrepreneurs to capture the returns from their innovations. This intuition is so deeply embedded in the literature that most empirical studies (Angulo-Guerrero et al. (2017), Fuentelsaz et al. (2015), McMullen et al. (2008) assume the relationship is linear. McMullen et al. even found that among all economic freedom components, only property rights showed a significant impact, and Aidis et al. (2006) concluded that property rights “dominate all other institutional variables” in predicting who becomes an entrepreneur. But every one of these studies assumed linearity. The data tell a more nuanced story.


This paper proposes and tests a U-shaped (nonlinear) relationship between property rights enforcement and total early-stage entrepreneurial activity (TEA). The theoretical framework draws on Austrian economics to explain why. Entrepreneurs perform economic calculation based on present facts and expectations about the future (Mises, 1949). Institutions lower uncertainty and provide stable ground for decision-making (North, 1990). When property rights are weak, there is an unknown but real cost of losing one’s property, which discourages risk-taking (Alchian, 2006). But simultaneously, high institutional uncertainty forces people into entrepreneurship as a last resort, what GEM calls necessity-driven entrepreneurship, where individuals “feel compelled to start their own business because all other options for work are either absent or unsatisfactory” (Reynolds et al., 2002). As institutions begin to improve, formal job opportunities absorb some of this necessity-driven activity, causing a decline in overall entrepreneurship. But beyond a threshold, improved enforcement increases confidence in long-term returns, lowers transaction costs, and incentivizes ventures based on genuine market opportunity. The interplay of declining necessity and rising opportunity entrepreneurship creates the U-shape.


The empirical analysis uses panel data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor across 90 countries from 2004 to 2018 (822 observations), paired with the Fraser Institute’s Legal System and Property Rights sub-index. The baseline specification is a random-effects panel regression of TEA on property rights and its square, controlling for GDP per capita (PPP), real GDP growth, unemployment, and population growth, with year dummies. The Hausman test did not reject the null, supporting the random-effects specification. Countries with fewer than three observations were dropped from the sample.





The U-shaped relationship: predicted TEA (solid curve) is driven by declining necessity entrepreneurship and rising opportunity entrepreneurship as property rights improve.




The results confirm the U-shape. The linear term on property rights is negative and highly significant (−5.590, p<0.01), while the quadratic term is positive and significant (+0.418, p<0.05). A Wald test confirms the squared term is significantly different from zero (p = 0.011). The minimum of the U occurs at a property rights score of approximately 6.69, comparable to Chile in 2018. Crucially, a purely linear specification yields an insignificant coefficient (−0.506, p>0.1), demonstrating that the linear model misses the true relationship entirely. The R-squared for the main specification is 0.448.


Separate regressions on opportunity-driven and necessity-driven entrepreneurship reveal the mechanism with precision. Each additional point in property rights increases opportunity entrepreneurship by 0.0432 percentage points (p<0.01) while decreasing necessity entrepreneurship by 0.0142 percentage points (p<0.01). The gain in opportunity ventures is more than three times the decline in necessity ventures, which is why the U-shape bends upward. However, the economic magnitude is modest: the difference between maximum and minimum predicted TEA is 6.27 percentage points (0.84 standard deviations), but this requires property rights to move 2.59 standard deviations, from Cameroon’s level (2.81) to Chile’s (6.69). All results are robust to substituting the World Bank’s Rule of Law estimate for the Fraser Institute measure.


The policy implications are important and underappreciated. Policymakers in developing countries should not be discouraged if modest institutional improvements do not immediately produce a surge in business creation. The initial decline in total entrepreneurship reflects a healthy structural transformation: the erosion of survivalist informality. The payoff comes only with sustained reform that pushes institutional quality past the trough. Countries stuck at intermediate levels, with enough regulation to suppress informal activity but not enough institutional quality to foster opportunity-driven ventures, face a genuine policy challenge. The path forward is not to relax enforcement, but to continue building the institutional foundations that attract productive entrepreneurship.






Fiscal & Monetary Policy Working Paper


Debt Constraints in Emerging Economies: Synthetic Control Evidence from Guatemala


 



Can institutional rules credibly constrain fiscal policy in a developing country? This question is central to the political economy of public finance. The theoretical case for fiscal rules is well established; without binding constraints, governments face systematic incentives to overborrow, exploit central bank financing, and shift costs to future taxpayers. But whether rules actually bind in practice, and whether headline improvements in fiscal outcomes reflect genuine discipline or something else entirely, is a question that demands careful empirical scrutiny.


Guatemala provides a compelling natural experiment. During the 1980s, the country experienced a severe macroeconomic crisis: inflation peaked at 60%, the fixed exchange rate collapsed in 1989, and the government relied heavily on central bank credit to finance persistent deficits. In response, two landmark reforms were adopted. A 1991 Monetary Board resolution limited net government borrowing from the central bank. Then, in 1993, a constitutional amendment went further, outright prohibiting central bank credit to the government, one of the most stringent fiscal rules adopted by any developing country in the period.


The paper uses the synthetic control method to evaluate these reforms. The outcome variable is central government debt as a percentage of GDP, drawn from the IMF Global Debt Database. The donor pool consists of 17 countries from Latin America (Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Paraguay), Asia (Bangladesh, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Thailand), and Africa (Botswana, Cameroon, Kenya, Morocco, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda), all selected to exclude countries with similar fiscal rule interventions, dollarization, or currency boards during the study period. The pre-treatment window runs from 1970 to 1990, and the post-treatment period extends through 2004. Predictor variables include real GDP per capita, population, gross fixed capital formation, government consumption, inflation, and three lagged values of the debt-to-GDP ratio. The synthetic Guatemala is composed primarily of Belize (29%), El Salvador (23%), Bangladesh (22%), Paraguay (21%), and Uganda (5%), and achieves a strong pre-treatment fit with an RMSPE of 3.87.






Guatemala’s actual debt-to-GDP versus its synthetic counterfactual. Hover to see exact values at each year.





Treatment effects (gap between actual and synthetic debt-to-GDP) with p-values. Hover to see exact values and significance levels.



After 1991, Guatemala’s debt-to-GDP ratio declines sharply while the synthetic counterfactual remains elevated, producing an average treatment effect of approximately −15 percentage points and a maximum gap of nearly 25 percentage points by the early 2000s. Statistical significance is limited in the initial post-treatment years, a common feature of synthetic control studies with small donor pools, but strengthens markedly in the later periods, with effects reaching significance at the 1% level from 2001 through 2003.


The headline result looks like a policy success. But the paper’s key contribution is disentangling the mechanism behind the improvement. Central bank debt did fall dramatically, from $0.9 billion in 1990 to $0.1 billion by 2000, confirming that the constitutional prohibition effectively eliminated that specific financing channel. However, total external debt actually increased from $2.6 billion to $3.3 billion over the same period. The government did not stop borrowing; it simply shifted to non-central-bank sources. The debt-to-GDP improvement came primarily because nominal GDP nearly tripled, driven by cumulative inflation of 123% and surging remittance inflows that rose from $130 million to $563 million and helped sustain the managed exchange rate.


The lesson is a cautionary one. Narrow fiscal rules can bind on their specific target; Guatemala’s constitutional prohibition on central bank lending was credibly enforced, but narrow rules do not guarantee broader fiscal discipline. Governments facing borrowing constraints on one margin can substitute toward others. And improving debt-to-GDP ratios can mask rising absolute debt levels when nominal GDP growth, driven by inflation, outpaces new borrowing. Evaluating fiscal rules requires looking at mechanisms, not just outcomes. Comprehensive frameworks covering total government borrowing, not just central bank financing, may be necessary to achieve genuine fiscal consolidation in emerging economies.
